guide.title: About MP4 and OGV
guide.markdown:
### What is an MP4 file?

MP4 is Part 14 of the MPEG-4 standard, ISO/IEC 14496-14, first published in 2003. QuickTime is where the design began and the ISO Base Media File Format carried it on, so the data is stored in nested boxes, which QuickTime calls atoms. As a container instead of a codec, MP4 is able to hold subtitles and chapters alongside the picture and sound. H.264 (AVC) video with AAC audio is the usual pairing, though AV1, VP9, MP3 and Opus can also appear inside.

Phone and camera recordings, downloaded clips and web video often come as MP4, and every major browser plays it. The endings .mp4 and .m4v mark video, while .m4a is common for audio-only MPEG-4. The two registered media types are video/mp4 and audio/mp4. From version 5.0 onward, Android plays HEVC video held in MP4.

### Programs that open MP4 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - mpv, an open desktop player, plays MP4 with selectable audio and subtitle streams.
  - ffplay, bundled with FFmpeg, includes the MP4 demuxer; playback also needs the matching decoders.
- **Windows and Mac:**
  - Adobe Premiere imports MP4 when the necessary decoder is available.
- **Web:**
  - Firefox plays supported media directly; AAC and H.264 availability can depend on system codecs.
  - Chrome plays the web audio and MP4 pairings it supports, and which ones work depends on the codec within.
- **Mobile:**
  - On Android, VLC is free, and what it decodes depends on the media stored in the container. On iOS, VLC opens most movie formats and can connect to media on the device or the network.

### MP4 and OGV compared

- **Names and types**: .mp4 with video/mp4; .ogv with video/ogg.
- **Layout**: an MP4 is a tree of boxes. An Ogg stream starts with the bytes OggS.
- **Who looks after it**: MPEG and ISO for MP4; the Xiph.Org Foundation for Ogg.
- **Typical codecs**: H.264 and AAC in MP4. Theora video with Vorbis sound is one documented Ogg combination.
- **Where it plays**: every major browser plays MP4. Ogg video opens in VLC and Firefox, and FFmpeg can read Ogg streams.

Nothing is copied across unchanged. FFmpeg decodes the video and writes it out again, which makes the OGV a fresh encode. The page passes no codec settings for .ogv, so FFmpeg's defaults apply: Theora video with Vorbis audio, and the video rate stays at its 200 kbit/s default. Frames marked as interlaced are deinterlaced on the way. The picture is fitted inside 1920 pixels, frames above 30 per second are dropped to reach 30 (the clip keeps its length), and the final size is forced to even numbers, which turns a 1279 by 719 source into 1278 by 718.

### Other ways to convert MP4 to OGV

- **FFmpeg:** `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -c:v libtheora -c:a libvorbis output.ogv` names the codecs outright, Theora for the picture and Vorbis for the sound, and writes them into an Ogg file. FFmpeg has to be built with libtheora and libvorbis support. Unlike this page, the command leaves the size and frame rate alone, so a large source stays large.
- **VLC media player:** From a terminal, `vlc sample.mp4 --sout="#transcode{acodec=vorb,vcodec=theo}:std{access=file,mux=ogg,dst=sample_new.ogv}"` transcodes with VLC's own encoders and writes sample_new.ogv. VLC's manual explains that the container must change because Theora and Vorbis are not compatible with MP4, and it shows the chain with an .ogg name for the same payload; .ogv is the ending Xiph recommends for Ogg video.
- **ffmpeg2theora:** `ffmpeg2theora input.mp4 -o output.ogv` uses a converter made for Ogg Theora and Vorbis. Its man page says it converts any media file that ffmpeg can decode, and that `-o` sets the output name; leave it out and the file is named after the input with an .ogv ending.

### Problems with MP4 files

- **An MP4 opens but shows no picture**: support for the container alone does not promise that your player can decode the video or the sound stored in it. Try another player, or convert the file here.
- **An MP4 has no sound to extract**: a file without an audio track leaves nothing for an audio editor to take.
- **The file will not play at all**: an interrupted write can leave an unfinished MP4 unplayable, because a normal MP4 keeps its packet metadata together. Record or fetch the file once more.

guide.title: About PNG and AVIF
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

GIF relied on a patented algorithm, and PNG (Portable Network Graphics) was created to replace it for lossless web images. In October 1996 PNG became the first format to be published as a W3C Recommendation; RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948 followed. A file starts with a fixed signature, then runs in chunks: IHDR holds the header, IDAT carries the image data and IEND closes the file. Its compressor is DEFLATE, which pairs LZ77 matching with Huffman codes, and no pixel data is thrown away.

Samples can be 1 to 16 bits wide, in indexed, grayscale or truecolor images, with an optional alpha channel. The current specification also describes animated PNG (APNG); a viewer without animation support displays a single fallback frame. Since June 2025 the third edition has been a W3C Recommendation; it introduces HDR signaling through a cICP chunk and a place for Exif data, the eXIf chunk. Screenshots, interface art and logos that need clear backgrounds are the typical material, and macOS saves screenshots as PNG by default. PNG is not known to be covered by royalty-bearing patents, and every big browser can show it.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP imports a PNG for editing.
  - ImageMagick reads PNG from the command line.
- **Web and Mobile:**
  - Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:**
  - Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari displays PNG.

### PNG and AVIF compared

- **Names and types**: PNG files end in .png (image/png, or image/apng for animated ones). AVIF files end in .avif.
- **Compression**: PNG is lossless without exception. AVIF stores AV1-compressed images in the HEIF container and can be lossy or lossless.
- **Alpha**: both support alpha transparency.
- **Depth**: a PNG sample is 1 to 16 bits wide. AVIF supports 10-bit and 12-bit depth, aimed at HDR and wide-gamut pictures.
- **Motion**: PNG has APNG; AVIF can hold image sequences.
- **Metadata**: since its third edition, PNG allows Exif data in an eXIf chunk.
- **Support**: every major browser shows PNG. Chrome 85 and Firefox 93 were the first to decode AVIF, Safari on iOS 16 added still AVIF images, and Android 12 and later decode baseline 8-bit AVIF. A browser that decodes AVIF does not guarantee that every app or operating system viewer opens the same file.

The page decodes the PNG with the browser's own decoder into 8-bit RGBA pixels and encodes those pixels as AVIF. That is why an animated PNG contributes only its first frame and no metadata is copied. The encoder is the browser's canvas where the browser can write AVIF, and ImageMagick where it cannot. AVIF is used for web images that need small files and for HDR and wide-gamut images.

### Other ways to convert PNG to AVIF

- **GIMP:** Open the PNG in GIMP, press Shift+Ctrl+E for File > Export As and pick AVIF as the type. GIMP added AVIF import and export in release 2.10.22, and its news post says HEIF files, AVIF included, can be handled at 10 and 12 bits per channel, so older releases lack the AVIF exporter.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick input.png output.avif` is the form ImageMagick's command-line page shows for converting one file into another format. Its formats page lists AVIF as readable and writable.
- **libavif avifenc:** `avifenc -q 80 input.png output.avif` calls libavif's own encoder, whose syntax line accepts jpg, jpeg, png and y4m input. Its `-q` option sets quality on the tool's own scale, up to a top value that means lossless. Add `--lossless` to set every default for lossless encoding; the tool emits warnings when the input or other settings do not allow it.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Changing the compression setting does not change the pixels**: PNG is lossless, so a different setting only changes how hard the encoder works.
- **Layers land in odd places in another program**: GIMP's PNG offset option can position layers differently elsewhere, so it is best left off.
- **Camera tags and profiles have gone**: GIMP leaves them out of an export unless you switch on its metadata controls.
- **An animated PNG shows a still picture**: this converter reads only the first frame of the file.
- **A 16-bit PNG loses depth here**: the converter passes 8-bit pixels to the encoder, so extra bits in the source do not reach the AVIF.

guide.title: About PNG and DOCX
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

A PNG records an image as a grid of pixels. Whether it holds a screenshot, a scanned letter, a diagram or a logo with see-through corners, the format knows nothing of words, so a screenshot of a paragraph is colored dots and not text.

PNG began as a patent-free replacement for GIF. The World Wide Web Consortium published it as a Recommendation in October 1996, and ISO published it as standard 15948. It compresses with DEFLATE without losing data, stores 1 to 16 bits per sample and may include an alpha channel. A file starts with a fixed signature and then runs in chunks. PNG is the usual choice for screenshots, interface graphics, logos with transparent areas and any web image that must stay crisp, and macOS saves its screenshots as PNG by default. The current specification also covers animated PNG, and its third edition, a W3C Recommendation since June 2025, allows Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk. PNG carries no known royalty-bearing patents, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP, a free editor, imports PNG for editing.
  - ImageMagick, a command-line tool, reads PNG.
- **Web and Mobile:**
  - Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:**
  - Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari displays PNG.

### PNG and DOCX compared

- **Names**: .png for the image, .docx for the document.
- **Purpose**: DOCX has been Microsoft Word's default format since Word 2007, and people use it for letters, reports, resumes and contracts. It can hold styles, images, tables, tracked changes and comments.
- **What each stores**: a PNG is one picture. A DOCX is a ZIP-based Open XML package with document parts and media parts, and an image sits in a part of its own.
- **Standards**: DOCX is specified in ECMA-376 and ISO/IEC 29500, while PNG answers to ISO/IEC 15948 and the W3C.
- **Text**: a PNG holds pixels, while the DOCX can hold typed text, styles and tables. This page writes none of that: pixel data differs from document text and layout.
- **Transparency**: a PNG can have an alpha channel, and the DOCX carries the PNG data unchanged.

The page makes a new Word document with one paragraph holding your PNG as an inline picture. Each pixel counts as one 96th of an inch, and a picture too big for the box of 6.5 by 9 inches is shrunk, with its proportions kept, until it fits. It never grows beyond its own size. The PNG is not re-encoded, and no text is recognized from it. You can pick several PNG files at once, and each one becomes its own DOCX while your originals stay as they were.

The DOCX is a document that holds your picture and nothing more. The PNG does not become text, a table or shapes you can edit, so a screenshot of a report stays a screenshot. If you need the words in it, extract the text separately and paste it into the document.

### Other ways to convert PNG to DOCX

- **Microsoft Word:** Start a blank document, use Insert > Pictures > This Device and select the picture, then use File > Save a Copy, updating the name and file type if needed.
- **LibreOffice Writer:** Choose Insert > Image and leave the Link box unchecked, so you keep working with the copy made when the picture was inserted; a linked bitmap is reloaded whenever the document loads. Then use File > Save As and pick Word 2010-365 Document (.docx) from the File type list. LibreOffice warns that saving to an external file type can lose some formatting.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Words in the image cannot be selected**: the picture holds pixels and not text, so any words must be typed or pulled out by other means before they can be selected.
- **A wide PNG looks small on the page**: a broad picture is scaled down, and its lettering shrinks with it. Crop the PNG first.
- **A smaller compression setting does not lower quality**: PNG compression is lossless, so the pixels stay the same at any setting.
- **Layer offsets differ between programs**: GIMP's PNG offset option can place layers differently in other applications, so avoid it.
- **Camera tags and profiles are missing**: GIMP exports leave them out unless you enable the relevant metadata controls.

guide.title: About PPTX and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PPTX file?

PPTX is PowerPoint's ordinary presentation document type. Since PowerPoint 2007 it has been a ZIP package of XML parts, standardized as Office Open XML (ECMA-376, ISO/IEC 29500), and PresentationML is the part of the standard that stores the slides. Each slide and its relationships occupy parts of their own, and notes and slide masters have XML parts too. Macro-enabled decks use .pptm instead.

Slide decks, training material and sales presentations are the usual PPTX files. A deck can also carry embedded media and charts, along with speaker notes and animations.

### Programs that open PPTX files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - LibreOffice Impress has a PowerPoint 2007-365 XML filter for import and export.
- **Windows and Mac:**
  - Microsoft PowerPoint opens and saves PPTX, its native presentation type.
- **Mac and iPhone:**
  - Keynote opens a PowerPoint presentation dragged onto its icon on a Mac, and on an iPhone it opens .pptx and .ppt documents.
- **Linux:**
  - ONLYOFFICE Desktop Editors is a desktop editor for Linux that opens PPTX.
- **Web:**
  - PowerPoint for the web supports PPTX presentations.
- **Mobile:**
  - The mobile PowerPoint app opens PPTX presentations.

### PPTX and JPG compared

- **Names and types**: .pptx with application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation; .jpg or .jpeg for the image.
- **Contents**: a PPTX is a package of slides, masters, notes and relationships. A JPG is one picture.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy, a format designed for photographs, with adjustable quality.
- **Alpha and layers**: JPG has no alpha channel and cannot store layers.
- **Editing**: saving a slide as an image turns its objects into one flattened picture, so the text is no longer editable.

The page draws each slide as SVG with a renderer that runs in your browser, then encodes the picture as a JPG at double the slide's dimensions in points. Lettering is set in the fonts the slide names, with metric-compatible fallbacks, and uses fonts installed on your device. The page leaves out hidden slides, speaker notes and comments. Video, and a picture the slide only links to, are not drawn either, and the page counts what was left out. The renderer numbers slides from its own list, so a hidden slide is never drawn in place of a visible one.

A JPG is a single flat picture, so the conversion turns a slide into what it looks like on the screen and nothing else. Text that was editable is now pixels, and notes are left behind. Keep the PPTX as your source if you still need to edit the deck.

### Other ways to convert PPTX to JPG

- **PowerPoint for Windows:** Select a slide, then use File > Save As (Save a Copy if the presentation is on OneDrive or SharePoint), type a file name, open the Save as Type list and choose JPEG, then press Save. Pick Just This One to save the selected slide, or All Slides for the whole deck, in which case Microsoft's help page says every slide becomes its own file.
- **PowerPoint for Mac:** Open the slide in Normal view, choose File > Export, pick JPEG as the image format, choose Save Current Slide Only and optionally set the width and height, then click Export.
- **Keynote for Mac:** Keynote opens PowerPoint files with a .pptx or .ppt ending. Choose File > Export To > Images, choose the slides you want, select an image format and click Save, then choose a location from the Where menu and click Export. Higher image quality produces a larger file. If the deck uses fonts you do not have installed, Keynote shows a missing font notification so you can choose replacements.

### Problems with PPTX files

- **Fonts or line breaks differ**: a font that is not installed can change how a deck looks, which is why PowerPoint offers to embed eligible fonts. This page draws slides with the fonts on your device and fallbacks.
- **An old .ppt or protected file is refused**: only an unprotected .pptx works here.
- **Video or linked pictures are missing**: neither is drawn, so they are left out of the JPG.
- **Hidden slides do not appear**: slides marked hidden are skipped, but their numbers still count in the file names.
- **A long deck stops partway**: the drawing is stopped after 90 seconds.
- **Features disappear in an older format**: saving as an older presentation format can affect features that format does not have.

guide.title: About PSD and JPEG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PSD file?

PSD is Adobe Photoshop's native document file format. Layers, masks, adjustment layers, text and color settings are stored so that a design stays editable. A file begins with the signature 8BPS and is arranged in sections, one section holding image resources and another the layer and mask data. Pixel data inside may be stored raw or packed with RLE or ZIP, and the header permits sample depths of one, eight, 16 or 32 bits.

The format allows at most 30,000 pixels in each direction, and anything larger has to be saved as PSB. Layered image editing, design mockups and photo retouching are what PSD files are made for. Its registered media type is image/vnd.adobe.photoshop, and a PSD can use CMYK or RGB color modes with 16-bit and 32-bit channels, and it is a proprietary Adobe format, so editors other than Photoshop read it through their own interpretation of the specification.

### Programs that open PSD files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - ImageMagick reads PSD images.
  - XnView MP lists PSD among its supported image formats; company use requires a license.
- **Web:**
  - In Photopea, PSD is the document type it is built around, and File > Open loads one.

### PSD and JPEG compared

- **Names and types**: PSD files end in .psd (image/vnd.adobe.photoshop). JPEG files use .jpg or .jpeg, two endings for one format.
- **Layers**: Photoshop keeps every layer and mask separate, while a JPEG holds a single flat image.
- **Compression**: PSD pixel data can be raw, RLE or ZIP encoded. JPEG is lossy, designed for photographs, with adjustable quality.
- **Use**: JPEG, a standard from the Joint Photographic Experts Group published as ISO/IEC 10918-1, serves photographs on the web, digital camera output and email attachments, and it is supported everywhere. PSD serves layered image editing.
- **Alpha**: a JPEG has no alpha transparency.
- **Depth**: PSD samples come in widths of 1, 8, 16 or 32 bits.
- **Size ceiling**: a PSD stops at 30,000 pixels per side, and PSB raises that limit.

ImageMagick's PSD reader hands back a single image, so a document with many layers yields one JPEG rather than a set per layer. No quality value is passed in by the page, and nothing is removed deliberately. The JPEG is a flat picture, and the editable layers stay in the PSD. You can choose several PSD files together; they convert one after another, and each JPEG downloads on its own, with no ZIP. The conversion does not change the PSD itself. The JPEG is named after the PSD with a .jpeg ending, and one PSD gives one JPEG.

### Other ways to convert PSD to JPEG

- **Photopea:** Photopea opens files through File > Open, and its File > Export As > JPG entry saves the picture as a JPG; the Save for Web window lets you choose the output format and the resolution. It runs in a browser tab. Photopea's help says every file you open there, such as PNG, JPG or Sketch, is converted to PSD.
- **XnConvert:** Drag the PSD into the Input tab, choose the target format, with its quality settings and a destination folder, on the Output tab, and click Convert. XnView's format list shows PSD as Adobe Photoshop with the psd extension, and JPEG as JPEG / JFIF. XnConvert's page names PSD as a format it can read, and the progress report lists any files that failed.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick 'input.psd[0]' output.jpeg` selects the first image of a file that holds several, since the index starts at zero. Quote the file name: the square brackets are special characters in most shells.

### Problems with PSD files

- **The page says the picture is too large**: shrink the document in Photoshop and export again.
- **The PSD is over 30,000 pixels wide**: a bigger document has to be saved as PSB or in some other format that allows more.
- **The result looks flat**: a JPEG cannot hold layers or masks. Keep the PSD for editing.
- **The picture looks different from Photoshop**: third-party readers must interpret Photoshop-specific data structures, and seeing a preview does not prove the file will edit the same way. Export from Photoshop when exact output matters.
- **You expected one JPEG per layer**: the converter takes one image out of the file, so a layered PSD gives a single JPEG. Separate layers need an editor that opens the PSD itself.

guide.title: About XCF and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is an XCF file?

The GNU Image Manipulation Program (GIMP) stores an image between editing sessions as XCF. It is the native format of GIMP, and it retains layers and transparency, channels, paths and selections rather than only a flattened picture. GIMP's documentation calls it the only format that can store everything about an image, with the exception of undo information, which is left out of the saved project.

In GIMP, the Save command writes XCF, while every other image format is made with Export. GIMP does not offer XCF as a format for exchange, and ordinary image viewers mostly cannot read it. That explains why people end up holding a file they cannot open: they download artwork that a designer shared as a working file, or they find an old project, and now need a picture to post, print or send. A JPG is the quickest answer, because JPG is supported everywhere.

Exporting does not modify the image itself, so the XCF stays as it was and nothing is lost by making a copy. Treat the XCF as the master and the JPG as the copy you hand to other people. Only the XCF lets you change a layer later.

### Programs that open XCF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP is the native project editor for XCF, and saving as XCF preserves the working image.
  - ImageMagick reads XCF, though nobody should assume its rendering reproduces every GIMP feature.

Most other image viewers cannot open XCF at all, which is why exporting a copy is the usual way to share the picture.

### XCF and JPG compared

- **Names and types**: .xcf for a GIMP image; .jpg or .jpeg for JPG, which are the same format.
- **Layers**: XCF keeps layers, channels, paths and selections. JPG cannot keep an editable stack of layers.
- **Compression**: XCF is lossless. JPG is lossy, with adjustable quality.
- **Transparency**: XCF retains it. JPG has no alpha transparency.
- **Standard**: JPG comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, was published as ISO/IEC 10918-1 and suits photographs.
- **Support**: a JPG shows up in every web browser, in Preview on macOS and in Windows Photos, while XCF belongs to GIMP.

This converter reads the XCF with ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly, so everything happens in your browser and no file leaves your device. ImageMagick takes a single image from the file, so a project with many layers still gives one JPG instead of a set. The page passes no quality value and strips nothing deliberately, so ImageMagick's own defaults apply. Each download is named after your original with a .jpg ending, and your XCF itself is never changed.

Because JPG cannot hold transparency, an XCF with see-through areas is a poor fit for this target. If you need to keep transparency, convert to PNG instead. Choose JPG for photographs and for pictures that you only need to show, where a smaller file is worth giving up exactness. Keep the XCF so you can come back to the layers.

### Other ways to convert XCF to JPG

- **GIMP:** Open the XCF in GIMP and use Export from the File menu to write the picture as JPEG. A dialog then lets you set the quality, which is the one control this page leaves out. Save the project separately if you want to keep edits.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick input.xcf -background white -flatten output.jpg` merges the images in the file into a single one. ImageMagick's documentation describes -flatten as creating a canvas in the current background color and compositing each image onto it, so any clear area shows white here. Inspect the result, since the rendering can differ from what GIMP shows.

### Problems with XCF files

- **Other programs cannot open the XCF**: most image viewers cannot read it. Export a copy from GIMP or convert it on this page.
- **The JPG has no transparency**: JPEG drops see-through pixels. If you need them, choose a format with an alpha channel, for example PNG.
- **Layers are missing from the JPG**: a JPEG is flat, so retain the XCF for future editing.
- **The JPG looks different from GIMP**: a third-party reader may not reproduce every feature. Export from GIMP when an exact match matters.
- **GIMP still asks to save after an export**: exporting does not save changes to the XCF project, so the warning on closing is expected. Save the XCF as well.
- **Quality numbers differ between editors**: two editors given one quality number may compress differently and produce a different look.
- **The page says the image is too large**: reduce the canvas size in GIMP first, then convert the smaller file.

guide.title: About 3GP and MP3
guide.markdown:
### What is a 3GP file?

The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), which writes the standards for mobile networks, defined 3GP as a container. MP4 grows from the same ISO base media file format; 3GP is a slimmed-down branch of it that keeps files small. Mobile messaging, downloads and packet-switched streaming are the services it was written for.

Inside one 3GP you may find video, speech, other sound and timed text. For the picture the specification registers H.263, MPEG-4 Visual, AVC and HEVC, and for the sound AMR variants and AAC. Brands in a file-type box tell a reader which profile a file follows, and the media type is video/3gpp when pictures are present or audio/3gpp when only sound is. You will mostly meet 3GP as video from older mobile phones and as MMS video.

Nothing in the extension tells you which permitted codec a recording uses. A parser that follows the specification may also skip boxes or codecs it does not define, so two files ending in .3gp can behave differently in one player.

### Programs that open 3GP files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - VLC media player lists 3GP among the input formats it opens.
  - FFmpeg reads 3GP containers.

A 3GP made of sound alone has no picture to recover, and the format expressly allows such files.

### 3GP and MP3 compared

- **Names and types**: .3gp (video/3gpp, or audio/3gpp for sound only) becomes .mp3.
- **Contents**: a 3GP can combine video, speech, sound and timed text, whereas an MP3 holds audio alone.
- **Compression**: sound in a 3GP is coded as an AMR variant or AAC. MP3 uses lossy audio coding, with constant or variable bitrate.
- **Metadata**: tags in an MP3 are stored as ID3 data.
- **Standard**: the MPEG group standardized MP3 as ISO/IEC 11172-3.
- **Support**: MP3 plays on nearly every device, including in any web browser.

The job is done by FFmpeg built for WebAssembly, running as a background worker in your tab, so the clip stays on your device. The command skips the video and hands the sound to LAME with a request for 192 kbps. Below 32 kHz sampling that request cannot be met: the ceiling is 160 kbps at 16 to 24 kHz and just 64 kbps at 8 to 12 kHz. Because the page leaves the sample rate alone, a narrowband recording produces a low-bitrate MP3. Channel count and stream choice are not set either, so FFmpeg's defaults apply, and with several tracks in a file the page does not tell you which one is taken.

Select as many 3GP files as you like. They are handled in sequence, and each MP3 arrives as its own download, with the original name plus .mp3. No ZIP is made, and the 3GP itself is left as it was. When a file is damaged or cut short, FFmpeg reports the error but still writes what it managed to read, so the MP3 is usually just shorter. If the 3GP has no audio track, the attempt ends in an FFmpeg exit-code error on the page.

Pulling out the sound cannot be undone in the MP3. It holds the audio and nothing else, so the picture stays behind in the 3GP. The encode is one more lossy step and cannot restore detail the original never held. The gain is a file that plays almost anywhere and is simple to share. For listening, that is a fair trade; for a recording you care about, keep the 3GP.

### Other ways to convert 3GP to MP3

- **FFmpeg:** `ffmpeg -i input.3gp -vn -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k output.mp3` mirrors what this page runs. FFmpeg's documentation lists -vn as the switch that disables video, -c:a as the audio codec option and -b:a as the audio bitrate option; swap 192k for another number to choose your own rate. The 3GP needs an audio stream that FFmpeg can decode.

### Problems with 3GP files

- **The conversion fails**: the likely cause is a 3GP with no audio track, which leaves nothing to extract. Play it in VLC first to check.
- **The extension does not reveal the codec**: a .3gp may hold AMR or AAC sound. If a tool refuses the file, a conforming parser is allowed to ignore codecs outside the specification.
- **A player shows no video**: an audio-only 3GP has no video track, which the format permits.
- **You also want the picture**: convert to MP4 instead, which keeps the video.
- **The MP3 is shorter than the clip**: with a cut-short file, only the part FFmpeg could read is converted.
- **The MP3 bitrate is under 192 kbps**: the recording's sample rate causes that, as described earlier, and nothing has gone wrong.

guide.title: About AIFC and MP3
guide.markdown:
### What is an AIFC file?

Apple developed the Audio Interchange File Format family, and AIFF-C, usually written AIFC, extended it to compressed sound in August 1991. A file stores sampled audio in an AIFF-related wrapper, described by its channel count, sample width and sampling frequency. It can also include markers that identify positions within the recording.

Despite the C in the name, an AIFC may hold plain uncompressed samples. Python's documentation lists the compression identifiers NONE, ULAW, ALAW and G722. The format shares the AIFF container but allows optional compression, and it carries metadata chunks. People use it for compressed audio on macOS and in audio production workflows.

That flexibility is also the source of most trouble. A recognized AIFC wrapper can still contain a codec that a reader does not implement, so two files with the same extension may behave differently in the same program.

### Programs that open AIFC files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - FFmpeg reads AIFF-C through its AIFF demuxer, though decoding depends on the stored encoding.
  - ffplay uses FFmpeg libraries for playback.
- **Windows and Mac:**
  - Adobe Audition opens AIFC, including common compressed AIFF variants and files with up to 32 channels, but it does not promise every variant.

### AIFC and MP3 compared

- **Names and types**: .aifc, the compressed AIFF-C file, becomes .mp3.
- **Compression**: an AIFC may be plain PCM or use an encoding such as ULAW or ALAW. MP3 is lossy, so some information is always discarded.
- **Metadata**: AIFC supplies markers and metadata chunks; an MP3 keeps its tags as ID3 data.
- **Standard**: ISO/IEC 11172-3 is the MPEG specification for MP3, which most devices can play.
- **Bitrate**: MP3 can hold audio at one fixed rate or at a rate that varies.

Here FFmpeg is built for WebAssembly and executes inside a browser worker, which means your audio never leaves the device. Video is switched off, and LAME aims for a 192 kbps encode. Sound sampled under 32 kHz limits what MP3 can do, giving a ceiling of 160 kbps for 16 to 24 kHz material and 64 kbps for 8 to 12 kHz material. The page keeps the sample rate as it is, and it does not set the channel count or a stream either, so FFmpeg's defaults decide.

Several AIFC files can go in together and are processed in turn. Every MP3 downloads on its own under the original name with .mp3 added, nothing is zipped, and the AIFC stays untouched. File size is not capped and no timeout is set, so how long a lengthy recording takes depends on your device. When an AIFC is cut short, FFmpeg usually still produces output, since it logs the problem and writes whatever it could read; expect an MP3 shorter than the source.

Moving from AIFC to MP3 trades fidelity for convenience. An AIFC holding PCM keeps every sample, while the MP3 discards some information for good. The loss is permanent, so convert a copy and keep the AIFC if you ever intend to edit or master the audio. Editing an MP3 and exporting another MP3 adds a second lossy stage, which is why the original is worth keeping. If the recording will only be listened to, the MP3 is the more widely playable file.

### Other ways to convert AIFC to MP3

- **FFmpeg:** `ffmpeg -i input.aifc -b:a 192k -c:a libmp3lame output.mp3` produces an MP3 aimed at the same 192 kbps this page requests. In FFmpeg's documentation -c:a is the option for the audio codec and -b:a the option for its bitrate, so another value in place of 192k gives you a different rate. Whether FFmpeg can read the file still depends on the compression type inside the AIFC.

### Problems with AIFC files

- **FFmpeg stops with an error**: the AIFC may use an encoding its reader lacks. Re-export it from an audio editor as uncompressed audio.
- **The MP3 sounds slightly different**: MP3 is lossy, so keep the AIFC for editing and convert a copy.
- **You want a lossless copy**: choose an uncompressed format from an audio editor, because this MP3 is not lossless.
- **You need to edit the audio later**: work from the AIFC, then make the MP3 as the last step. A second lossy encode adds more loss.
- **Only part of the file converted**: a cut-short AIFC converts what could be read. Compare the lengths of both files before deleting the original.
- **Audition will not open it**: Audition opens common compressed AIFF variants but does not promise every one.
- **The MP3 comes out under 192 kbps**: a low sample rate causes it, as covered earlier, and nothing is broken.

faqs.answer: Not exactly. Nothing is enlarged, but a very large picture is reduced and a very high frame rate is thinned, and the final width and height are made even. The limits are listed in the guide below.

faqs.question: Is WMV the same as ASF?
faqs.answer: Related. They are the Windows Media members of the family, so the advice for ASF covers them.

faqs.question: Why won't my ASF play where I need it?
faqs.answer: The .asf extension identifies a wrapper and does not establish which audio or video decoder is needed. The MP4 made here holds H.264 and AAC instead.

faqs.question: Who made ASF?
faqs.answer: Microsoft created ASF as a proprietary, publicly documented wrapper for multimedia, designed for media delivery including streaming.

faqs.question: Why did the conversion fail?
faqs.answer: The page shows an FFmpeg exit-code error when FFmpeg cannot process the file. FFmpeg needs a decoder for each stream inside, and the extension does not say which ones those are.

faqs.question: How long can the video be?
faqs.answer: The page imposes no length limit and no timeout. How long a long video takes depends on your device, because FFmpeg runs in a single thread of the browser.

faqs.question: Can I use the MP4 instead of the original?
faqs.answer: For playback, yes. For editing or archiving, keep the ASF, since the MP4 is a re-encode.

guide.title: About ASF and MP4
guide.markdown:
### What is an ASF file?

Microsoft created Advanced Systems Format (ASF) as a proprietary but publicly documented multimedia wrapper. One file can hold audio, video, still images and other stream types, and the format was designed for media delivery, including streaming. It is used for Windows Media streaming and for WMV and WMA files.

WMA and WMV are subtypes of ASF associated with Windows Media streams, so a .wmv is the wrapper carrying Windows Media video. Titles, authorship, copyright and technical details can sit in header objects, and part of that may be digital rights management data, which is not the same thing as ordinary descriptive tags. The registered MIME type is application/vnd.ms-asf.

The extension names a wrapper only, and says nothing about the decoder the streams need. Picture fidelity and multichannel support depend on the encoded streams rather than on the ASF wrapper. Two files that end in .asf can therefore behave very differently in the same player.

### Programs that open ASF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - VLC media player lists ASF, WMV and WMA among its input formats.
  - FFmpeg supports ASF input and output, though decoders for the streams inside are still required.

### ASF and MP4 compared

- **Names and types**: .asf, which uses the MIME type application/vnd.ms-asf, becomes .mp4.
- **Wrapper**: ASF is a Microsoft design for streaming audio and video. MP4 comes from ISO/IEC 14496-14; it can store video, audio, subtitles and metadata together.
- **Codecs**: what an ASF carries depends on its streams. An MP4 can wrap many codecs; the pairing you meet most is H.264 picture with AAC sound.
- **Metadata**: ASF header objects carry titles and technical data, while an MP4 can hold metadata along with subtitles.
- **Support**: MP4 plays on nearly every device, so it is the safer container to hand to other people.

Your browser runs FFmpeg as WebAssembly in a worker, which keeps the ASF on your machine. The video is decoded and re-encoded by libx264 with the ultrafast preset, the zerolatency tune and a constant rate factor of 32, while the sound becomes AAC at 96 kbps. The file is also asked to carry its index at the front. Streams are chosen by FFmpeg's defaults, so for a file with several tracks the page cannot tell you which is taken.

Size and frame rate carry over up to a limit. Nothing is enlarged. When the longer side passes 1920 pixels the picture is reduced to fit, and both dimensions are trimmed to even numbers, so an odd side gives up one pixel. A source running above 30 frames a second drops frames yet keeps its duration, and a slower rate is left as it is.

Pick any number of ASF files. The page takes them in sequence, and every MP4 is saved separately with the original name plus .mp4. Nothing is zipped, and the ASF remains unchanged. No cap on size or time is applied, so a lengthy video is limited only by your device. If a file is damaged or ends abruptly, FFmpeg usually still writes an MP4 after logging the error, and the result is shorter than the source.

The video goes through a second encode, so the MP4 does not reproduce the original picture exactly. Keep the ASF if you plan to edit or archive, and treat the MP4 as the version you share.

### Other ways to convert ASF to MP4

- **FFmpeg:** `ffmpeg -i input.asf -c:v libx264 -c:a aac -movflags +faststart output.mp4` writes H.264 and AAC. FFmpeg's documentation explains that +faststart adds a second pass which relocates the index to the file's beginning. This command sets no preset or quality value, so libx264's own defaults apply rather than the speed-first choices this page makes. It transcodes the streams FFmpeg selects, so check a file with several streams instead of assuming every one survives.

### Problems with ASF files

- **The ASF will not play where you need it**: convert it to MP4.
- **The conversion fails**: check that the file plays in VLC, or get a fresh copy.
- **The MP4 looks soft**: the page uses a fast preset and offers no quality control; run FFmpeg yourself if you want other settings.
- **The picture shrank**: very large pictures are brought down to the page's size limit.
- **A WMV or WMA file will not open elsewhere**: the same advice holds for them.

faqs.question: How do I convert a CUR cursor to PNG?
faqs.answer: Choose the .cur file and save the PNG. Your browser decodes the cursor and the page writes the picture as PNG. Several files give one PNG each.

faqs.question: Does the cursor keep its transparency?
faqs.answer: Yes. The cursor's outline sits on a clear background in the PNG, because the page keeps transparency when it writes PNG.

faqs.question: What happens to the hotspot?
faqs.answer: It is dropped. The hotspot marks the active pointer pixel, and CUR stores its coordinates beside the image. The PNG has no field for it, so write the coordinates down before converting if you plan to rebuild a cursor.

faqs.question: My CUR has several sizes. Which one do I get?
faqs.answer: One PNG, not one for each size. To choose a size yourself, use ImageMagick on your own computer, which can select an image from the file by its index.

faqs.question: Can a PNG become a cursor again?
faqs.answer: Yes. The [PNG to CUR converter](/png-to-cur/) on this site makes a CUR from a PNG. A PNG has nowhere to keep a hotspot, so it has to be set again.

faqs.question: Does an animated cursor work?
faqs.answer: Animated cursors use the ANI format, not CUR, and this page reads CUR files.

faqs.question: Is the metadata kept?
faqs.answer: No. Only raw pixels reach the PNG writer, so metadata does not come along.

faqs.question: Is a CUR the same as an ICO?
faqs.answer: They are related, with CUR adding the active pointer position. For that target, use [CUR to ICO](/cur-to-ico/).

faqs.question: Does the PNG have a quality setting?
faqs.answer: No. PNG is lossless, so the page has no quality value to hand over when writing the file.

faqs.question: Why does the page say the picture could not be decoded?
faqs.answer: The browser could not decode the image, and the page shows "Image decode failed." If the message says your browser cannot open these files, switch to a current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.

guide.title: About CUR and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a CUR file?

Windows stores custom mouse pointers and cursor themes in the CUR container. Its layout resembles ICO, with the addition of coordinates for the active pointer location. Those coordinates name the hotspot, the one pixel treated as the click point.

A single CUR can hold images at different dimensions, and every one has its own hotspot data. Animated cursors belong to ANI and not to the usual CUR workflow. The format is built for pointer assets, so an ordinary image format fits better when you have no use for the hotspot, which is the usual reason for converting. When you convert a CUR, you are generally after the picture, for use as artwork, in documentation or as a reference.

The hotspot is the part that trips people up. A misplaced hotspot makes clicks land away from the visually expected point, and a multi-size cursor needs a valid hotspot in every embedded image. Copying coordinates blindly between sizes can misalign the pointer.

### Programs that open CUR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - ImageMagick lists CUR as a readable format, so you can use it to inspect or render cursor images.
- **Windows:**
  - Visual Studio Image Editor can view and edit cursor resources; 32-bit images can be viewed there but not edited.
- **Mac and Linux:**
  - XnView MP, a viewer that lists CUR as a supported format, costs nothing for private and educational use.

### CUR and PNG compared

- **Names and types**: .cur for a Windows cursor, .png for a Portable Network Graphics image.
- **Structure**: a CUR holds the same layout as an ICO, with a hotspot for each image and several sizes per file. A PNG holds one picture and no hotspot.
- **Transparency**: both can carry alpha transparency. PNG compression is lossless.
- **Standard**: PNG appeared in the mid-1990s to replace GIF without patent worries, and it is an ISO/IEC 15948 standard as well as a W3C Recommendation.
- **Support**: every browser displays PNG, while CUR mostly serves Windows pointers.

Your browser's own image decoder reads the CUR and hands the pixels to the page, which writes the PNG with a canvas. Transparency is kept and PNG has no quality setting, so nothing is traded away for file size. Pixels pass through as 8-bit RGBA, and since only pixels travel, metadata does not. The work happens in your browser, in a Web Worker that falls back to the main thread if the worker fails, so the file is not uploaded.

Several CUR files may be selected in one go. The page handles them in order and saves a PNG for each, named like the source but ending in .png. Nothing is zipped, the CUR files stay as they were, and the page applies no file-size cap of its own.

A PNG of a cursor is a picture only. It shows what the pointer looks like, but the click point is stored in the CUR and not in the PNG. That is fine for documentation, screenshots or a reference image, and it is the reason to keep the CUR if you plan to install the cursor again. The PNG also holds a single picture. If a CUR contains several sizes, use a tool from the list below to choose the one you want.

### Other ways to convert CUR to PNG

- **ImageMagick:** `magick 'input.cur[0]' output.png` names the first embedded image explicitly. ImageMagick's documentation says an index in square brackets selects an image from a multi-image file and that numbering starts at zero, so changing it to `[1]` takes the second image. ImageMagick lists CUR among the formats it reads.
- **Pillow:** `python3 -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('input.cur').save('output.png')"` saves the cursor as a PNG. Pillow's documentation says its CUR decoder reads the largest available cursor and that animated cursors are not supported. CUR is on its read-only list, so it can open the format but not write it.

### Problems with CUR files

- **Clicks land in the wrong place after you rebuild a cursor**: the hotspot is not stored in the PNG. Set it again in your cursor editor and check each frame's coordinates.
- **You wanted a different size**: the page saves one picture. Use ImageMagick with an index to pick another image from the file.
- **The page says decoding failed**: your browser could not read the file. Try another copy, or a current browser.
- **You only have an animated .ani cursor**: that is a separate format, and this page reads CUR.
- **A hotspot looks misplaced in your own cursor**: open the cursor in an editor and compare the point for each size.
- **You do not need the hotspot at all**: a conventional image format such as PNG is the better choice for artwork.
